summary_for_principal:
You asked me to pressure-test the grounded-inquiry workflow through the real engine, not just check its paperwork. It had never actually run before, only been checked as well-formed. Running it for real found and fixed four genuine bugs, all now covered by tests:

- Recording a finding sometimes crashed the whole run instead of cleanly failing just that step.
- Three bugs let a "try a couple more times, then move on" loop get stuck retrying forever, silently skip a needed re-check, or (the worst, found while double-checking the others) silently ignore a real approval decision in favour of a stale one. All now behave exactly as configured.

I also found the example's own "require a person's sign-off if confidence is too low" rule can never fire, since an earlier check already ends the run first — a gap in the example, not a live bug. Full suite: 342 tests passing.

Numbered actions:
1. Nothing needs your decision — implementation bugs, not judgment calls, so I found and fixed them all.
2. Found and left: the unreachable sign-off rule in the example (harmless).
3. Opinion: merge this, then connect a real AI reviewer to actually run this workflow.

decisions.headline: State writes that don't fit their channel's declared reducer (§2.3) are now checked before the attempt is durably recorded and refused cleanly (StepOutcome.STATE_MISMATCH), instead of being recorded SUCCESS and then crashing the caller when the write was actually applied.
decisions.problem: Driving the real Appendix A process for the first time found that MERGE/APPEND/UPSERT_BY_ID (§2.3) had never been implemented — engine/state.py only ever applied REPLACE — and that the one write path that existed recorded SUCCESS first, then raised an uncaught exception applying the mismatched write, crashing report() itself with no answer returned at all.
options_rejected: Record SUCCESS first, let a mismatched write fail some later call: rejected, the attempt is already durably SUCCESS by then and there is no way to un-record it (write-once, §12.2).

Invent a dedicated on_state_mismatch route field: rejected, §2.3 names no such field; INPUT_UNRESOLVED/NOT_DISPATCHABLE already establish the precedent for a structural failure with no dedicated route (falls through to a clean ended run).
Silently coerce the value to fit its reducer (e.g. wrap a scalar in a list for APPEND): rejected, invents a coercion rule nothing in the spec states.
decisions.cost_to_change: Low — the four reducer implementations are a literal reading of §2.3's own sentence; the routing choice (no dedicated field) is local to _route_for_step_failure.

evidence.claim: Before this fix, driving the real Appendix A process's `gather` step (an APPEND channel) crashed report() with an unhandled UnsupportedReducer exception, propagating uncaught rather than returning any NextAnswer.
evidence.source: Ad hoc repro script run against the real fixture, this run, before the fix; traceback captured directly.

evidence.claim: After the fix, the same script returns a clean TOOL_STEP hand-off with no crash, and a mismatched write (a bare string for an APPEND channel) ends the run cleanly as FAILED rather than crashing.
A real APPEND write accumulates correctly across two separate STEP nodes writing to the same channel.
All four reducers (REPLACE/MERGE/APPEND/UPSERT_BY_ID) apply correctly on an accepted write and raise ReducerMismatch on a bad-but-conformant one, per reducer.

untouched.divergence: sign-off declares person_required_when: 'state.confidence == "INSUFFICIENT"', but honest-stop (evaluated earlier in the same process) already routes confidence == INSUFFICIENT straight to the INSUFFICIENT ending, before recommend/check-fidelity/sign-off are ever reached — so this condition can never evaluate true in a real run of this process as written.
untouched.why_not_now: This is spec Appendix A's own worked example declaring a condition it can never need, not an engine bug — the person_required_when mechanism itself is separately correct and tested (tests/engine/test_gates.py). Fixing the example (picking a different, reachable condition, or removing the field) is a product/documentation decision about what the worked example should demonstrate, outside this pass's scope of finding and fixing real engine bugs.

untouched.divergence: produced_by only ever records an AGENT-attributed write (performed_by starting 'AGENT:...') and is never cleared or updated when a LATER CODE-attributed write (performed_by starting 'CODE:...') subsequently overwrites the same state path with a different value — so §7.6's 'no deciding on your own work' check can attribute a state path's CURRENT value to an agent identity that did not actually produce it, if a CODE step overwrote that agent's earlier write. Found while writing the sign-off agent-decider test: `recommend` (a SKILL step, AGENT-attributed) writes state.recommendations, which check-recommendation-fidelity (CODE) then overwrites — produced_by still names the original AGENT identity.
untouched.why_not_now: Whether the 'more correct' behaviour is to clear produced_by on any overwrite, or to attribute it to the CODE step (untracked), or to track both an original-drafter and a final-writer separately, is a product judgement call this pass has no mandate to make blind, and no fixture or scenario currently depends on the answer either way (the one test that touches this deliberately uses a distinct reviewer identity to sidestep it, and notes why in its own docstring).

lessons.maxim: When a fix corrects a baseline/counting bug in one node-type's replay logic, check every OTHER node type that shares the same replay contract before declaring the bug class closed — and check it with a real test, not by reasoning about why the other type is different.
lessons.incident: D20 fixed this bug class for STEP nodes and explicitly reasoned ROUTE was safe ('a ROUTE's own visit is always exactly one attempt') — true of any single visit, but not of how many unconsumed past visits could sit in the slice once a loop had looped back more than once. The very next thing built (the committed e2e suite) found ROUTE had the identical latent bug (D21), whose own regression test had, unnoticed, encoded the bug's wrong behaviour as its expected assertion. D21's own reasoning then repeated the SAME mistake in the opposite direction: its Consequences field said this applied to 'a ROUTE (not a GATE)', reasoning GATE was safe from unstructured analysis rather than a test. Actually testing it (D22) found GATE had a related but worse bug — not skipping a node, but silently discarding a later, genuinely different decider verdict in favour of an earlier stale one. Two node types in a row were declared safe by reasoning and were wrong both times; only the third was actually verified before being declared safe, and only because it was tested rather than reasoned about.
lessons.destination: docs/spec/process-definition.md's own D20 entry now carries an Update annotation naming this correction directly, as the artefact this lesson changed.
lessons.proposed_check: Before closing out any future replay/baseline fix as covering 'every node type', write a test that drives the SAME bug shape past its actual boundary condition for every OTHER node type sharing the replay contract — never write a Consequences/Reversal claim that a sibling node type is unaffected without that test backing it.

The four bugs that made this impossible or unreliable before are fixed and each recorded as its own spec decision-log entry (D19-D22): a crash on any non-REPLACE state write, and three separate loop-replay bugs (STEP, ROUTE, GATE) that could stall a run, skip a step, or silently discard a real decision.
